Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The weekend comes from a shelf display that staff made last spring, when customers asked for more books about the older roads around Bellwether. The display became two shelves and then a series of short events, so the store is now putting several parts together across one weekend. It includes new books, used books, maps, and material from local contributors. The selection is not a complete history of the county, and the store has not described it that way. Store manager Lena Ortiz said, “We wanted the weekend to feel useful whether someone is planning a trip, tracing a family route, or simply curious about the names on a road sign.”

At noon, the meeting table will be used for an informal map-reading session led by staff member Nia Brooks. Visitors can bring a printed map they already own, but the store will also put out copies of a 1938 street map and a current city map. the session isn't a class and people can join or leave while it is happening. at 2 p.m. local travel writer Owen Pike will read from his new book, “The Northbound Mile,” and take questions. The reading is scheduled for 35 minutes, with questions after it.

2. Sunday starts with an 11:30 a.m. talk by archivist Priya Shah about the difference between a road name appearing in a directory and a road appearing on a map. She will show three examples from Bellwether directories dated 1912, 1926, and 1941. At 1 p.m. the shop is hosting a small table of map publishers and local makers, with printed walking maps from North Line Press, hand-drawn neighborhood cards by Eli Ward, and a table of used atlases selected by the bookstore. The publishers are selling their own items directly, and the bookstore will ring up the used books at its regular counter. There will not be a separate entrance or a separate ticket for the table.

There are several details about where things are, because the shop is narrow and readers should know what to expect. The talks take place at the long table in the back room, which has 18 chairs, and there is standing room along one wall for about six more people. Seating is first come, first served, and the store is not reserving seats by email or phone. The map-reading session also uses that room. The publisher tables will be set up near the front windows, not across the doorway, and the used atlases will be on the low table beside the fiction shelves. Staff will keep the aisle from the entrance to the checkout counter clear.

The building has one step at the front entrance and no automatic door. A portable ramp is available, and visitors who need it can call the shop at 555-0148 before arriving so a staff member can bring it to the door. The back room is on the same floor as the sales area, and there is a restroom in the rear hall. The restroom doorway is 28 inches wide. There is no designated event parking lot; two-hour street parking is available on Alder Street and the nearby blocks, subject to posted signs. The nearest bus stop is at Alder and Third, about two blocks away. The store does not have a bicycle rack, though public racks are on the library side of Third Street.

Cedar & Finch will have a display of books about regional routes and mapmaking in the front window from September 1 through September 20. The display includes new books from four publishers and used titles selected by bookseller Mateo Ruiz. Some used copies have notes or marks from previous owners, and those condition details are listed on their price labels. The store has 12 copies of “The Northbound Mile” in stock as of the announcement date, August 18. That number may change before the reading. Pike will sign copies after the questions, but the store is not taking advance payment or holding copies by request. The book can also be ordered through the shop if the copies sell out.

The event does not include a guided walking tour, despite the walking maps on the Sunday table. Staff will not lead groups outside the store, and the program does not require participants to use a phone or download an app. Visitors may take notes, but the historical examples shown by Shah are reproductions, not original archive records. The store has permission to show the reproduced pages during her talk. Anyone who wants to consult original records can ask Shah after the program for information about the Bellwether County Archive’s public reading room; archive access and hours are handled by the archive, not by the bookstore.

The Mill Street History Newsletter is prepared by a small volunteer team, but its work begins well before anyone opens a document to write. Each issue starts with a planning meeting at the library, where the editor, two regular contributors, and whoever can attend review possible topics. The group keeps a notebook of suggestions from readers, along with dates, names, and any leads that need checking. A note such as “the old bakery had a second floor” is useful as a starting point, but it is not treated as a fact until someone finds supporting evidence.

The team chooses one main story and, when space allows, a short item about a photograph, building, or family collection. Topics are judged partly by the material available and partly by whether readers can learn something specific from them. A broad subject such as “shops on Mill Street” may become a piece about the hardware store’s changing location, provided that the records support the narrower focus. The editor writes the proposed angle and a list of open questions on a planning sheet. Contributors can then see what remains uncertain before they begin gathering material.

1. Build a small, traceable source file

For each story, the contributor creates a folder with a simple name, such as “Mill Street hardware store.” The folder holds scans or photographs of relevant material, a source log, interview notes, and a draft. Each entry in the source log identifies the item, its owner or holding institution, its date if known, and the detail it supports. A directory listing, for example, might establish that a store occupied a particular address in 1948. It would not, by itself, establish why the business moved there.

The team consults town directories, local newspapers, maps, deeds, school records, and family papers when they are available. A date copied from an index is checked against the original page whenever possible. If two sources disagree, the contributor records both versions rather than choosing the more convenient one. The editor asks, “Can a reader follow this sentence back to something we actually saw?” That question helps distinguish a documented detail from a reasonable guess.

Digital copies are named with a short description and date, not left under a camera’s default filename. The original image remains unchanged, and a working copy can be cropped or brightened for reading. Contributors note when a scan is incomplete, blurry, or missing its reverse side. If a document is borrowed from a resident, the source log records who provided it and whether the team may reproduce it in the newsletter. A photograph shared for research is not automatically cleared for publication.

Interviews are arranged with a clear explanation of the newsletter’s purpose. Before recording, the interviewer asks whether the person is comfortable being recorded and whether their name may appear. The interviewer also checks spellings, approximate dates, and the names of people mentioned. Memories are valuable evidence of what someone recalls, but they are not silently presented as official records. A sentence such as “I remember the shop closing around 1962” remains an attributed memory unless another source verifies the date. If a speaker asks to review a quotation for accuracy, the contributor sends the relevant passage rather than the entire article for approval.

2. Draft, check, and prepare the issue

The first draft separates established details from unresolved ones. Bracketed notes such as “[check the address in the 1950 directory]” are useful during writing, but they must be resolved or removed before publication. The contributor avoids smoothing away meaningful uncertainty. If a source says “about 1905,” the article does not turn that into an exact year. If the evidence supports two possibilities, the text explains that the date is uncertain and identifies the conflicting records.

A second volunteer checks names, dates, addresses, quotations, and captions against the source file. This is a factual review, not an invitation to make the story more dramatic. The reviewer marks questions in the draft and cites the relevant source-log entry. The writer then answers each question or revises the passage. For a long quotation, the team checks the recording or notes against the published wording; punctuation may be adjusted for readability, but the speaker’s meaning is not changed.

The editor checks the layout after the text is settled. Captions are placed beside the correct images, and every image credit is included. The team uses a consistent format for dates and street names so that readers can compare entries across issues. If a contributor has permission to use an image only in print, the online version receives a different image or omits it. The production checklist includes a final review of links, page numbers, contrast, and contact details for corrections.

Before distribution, the editor keeps a dated copy of the approved issue and its source files in the newsletter archive. One copy is stored on the library’s shared drive, and another is saved to a separate backup device. The source log makes future corrections easier: if a reader points out that a shop stood at number 14 rather than number 12, the team can identify which record supplied the address and check it again. Corrections are dated and described in the next issue or on the newsletter’s archive page, depending on where the original item appeared.

Readers can send suggestions, corrections, and offers of material by email or leave a note at the library desk. The editor records each message and replies when a response is needed. A brief acknowledgment does not promise that a suggestion will become a story, and a family photograph may require further permission or research before it can be used. The newsletter’s practical aim is to make local material easier to understand and trace, while being candid about what the surviving evidence can and cannot establish.", "output": "A Working Process for the Mill Street History Newsletter
